items.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
items.summary: In New York, the Pentagon and Pennsylvania, solemn ceremonies commemorate the landmark anniversary.
items.content:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.

Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.

Two beams of light illuminated the Manhattan sky for a Tribute in Light on Friday evening, as other landmarks in the state lit up in blue in commemoration.

George W Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks, was joined by former Presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton at Friday's ceremony at the World Trade Center site.

At the Pentagon, President Trump attended a commemoration alongside cabinet secretaries and Condoleezza Rice, who was national security adviser on 9/11.

"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago," Trump said. "We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today."

He sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.

Trump told the crowd that the Islamic Republic "will never, ever have a nuclear weapon".

Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.

Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11

9/11: What happened and how many people died in September 11 attacks?

Janice Brooks had only moved to New York a couple of weeks before 9/11 to begin what she calls "the biggest adventure", working for a company on the 84th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

She told the BBC she was in the office when the first plane hit the North Tower. While she was evacuating, the second plane hit with an "almighty thud".

Brooks said she heard "one of those horror film screams" as a woman was hit by debris. She looked up and saw a "big gaping hole" where her office should have been.

Every year on 11 September, bells ring to commemorate the exact time that each of the four planes crashed, and the exact time the Twin Towers fell.

This year, a seventh bell was rung to commemorate the thousands who died from diseases including cancer after the attacks.

Illnesses related to dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have since claimed more than threefold the nearly 3,000 lives lost in the attacks, US health officials say.

As the names of the dead were read out for nearly four hours at the ceremony in Manhattan, a 9/11 widow criticised Saudi Arabia and what she characterised as failures by US officials to hold the kingdom accountable.

"You are missed more with each year that passes," Terry Strada said of her husband Tom Strada in remarks broadcast live worldwide.

"But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?"

You can listen to Terry Strada's story in the BBC radio documentary Intrigue: A 9/11 story

The comments by Strada, national chairperson of 9/11 Families United, drew applause from the audience.

The majority of those who carried out the 9/11 attacks were from Saudi Arabia and planning was led by al-Qaeda founder Osama Bin-Laden, scion of a prominent Saudi family.

But Saudi officials have repeatedly denied any involvement in the attacks, and in 2004 the 9/11 Commission Report "found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded" al-Qaeda.

Events were also held elsewhere to honour the victims. In London, there was a ceremonial event at Buckingham Palace attended by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the US ambassador Warren Stephens.

The Toronto Stock Exchange also held an event to remember colleagues who died in the attacks.

In Gander, Newfoundland, the US ambassador to Canada praised the small town that took in thousands of passengers from 38 diverted planes in the hours after the attack.

"When people in America hear the word Gander, our hearts soften," Pete Hoekstra said.

"As a representative of the United States government, thank you for your friendship... to the nation of Canada, thank you for being a partner and for the shared sacrifices that you made with us."

His remarks come amid fraught relations between the US and Canada, with the two countries engaged in a trade war. Ahead of the 9/11 commemorations, some Gander residents had called for Hoekstra's invite to be rescinded.

Still, Hoekstra's speech was met with applause. But in separate remarks afterwards, former Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chrétien said: "I have message for American friends... never mistake our generosity for weakness." He received a standing ovation.

In Milan, a group of Italian and US firefighters participated in a ceremonial stair climb to honour the emergency responders who died in the line of duty.

Dressed in their uniforms and carrying equipment, they climbed 110 floors up and down the Galfa Tower, in remembrance of the number of storeys on each of the Twin Towers.

'We never recovered him': Quest to identify remains from Ground Zero continues

'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on

Spies, strategies and missed opportunities: How the lessons of 9/11 are still being learnt

items.title: Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe
items.summary: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen.
items.content:
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.

Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.

And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October .

The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.

"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".

Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna , Bronze Age artefacts in Spain , and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about.

The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.

Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.

Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.

Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats.

"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."

The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show "a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes".

Data provided to the BBC by ARCA shows recorded museum thefts in France spiked in 2024, and rose again slightly in 2025.

However, numbers go up and down over time, with more thefts recorded in 2015 than a decade later.

These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public - although some people argue they steal "from the rich, who cares?" Brand says.

Others point out the colonial history behind many treasures in European museums, with art historians highlighting the French crown jewels stolen from the Louvre contained emeralds, diamonds, sapphires and pearls which are not native to France.

Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.

Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.

For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-Century mansions in Langres.

"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains.

Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.

And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.

Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month , external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.

What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so about 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says.

Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.

"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."

Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says.

After a theft, police generally have between four and six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators.

But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case.

On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them".

Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".

Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds.

After its theft in October, Maison des Lumières launched a security audit carried out by police officers appointed by France's cultural ministry, mayor Caviezel says.

Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed.

MAK in Vienna also increased its security to prevent "copycat offenders and to provide our audience with visible security", its director says. Entry is through a metal detector, and bags must be put in the cloakroom or in lockers, and there are more security guards.

Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.

"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."

Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine.

Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.

However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".

"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution."

Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.

Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months.

Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a Unesco convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged.

items.title: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
items.summary: Mountaineer Mingma G tells the BBC about the climb to bring home the bodies of his closest friends.
items.content:
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.

Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.

But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.

And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.

"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"

Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.

Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."

Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter .

Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.

The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.

Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.

Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.

In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.

Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."

But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".

Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".

This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.

Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.

On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.

By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.

At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.

The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.

The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".

"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.

The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.

The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.

By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.

One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.

Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.

But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.

Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.

He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.

It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".

Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.

He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.

"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."

Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.

They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.

But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.

When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".

Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.

The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.

Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.

The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.

There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.

On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.

With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.

The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.

The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.

The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.

Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.

The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.

Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.

"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."

items.title: OpenAI agents carried out an undisclosed attack on RubyGems
items.summary: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Sep/12/openai-agents-rubygems... Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49666735 Points: 786 # Comments: 436
items.content:
On May 11th, 2026, hundreds of malicious packages were uploaded to RubyGems by AI agents. We believe these were authored by internal OpenAI agents (more) .

We share our detailed findings below. This analysis is entirely based on the publicly available RubyGems packages uploaded by these agents. We also talked with RubyGems and rubydoc.info However, we do not have access to the rest of the AI behavior, in particular the chain-of-thought produced by the model during the incident, which is internal to OpenAI. Therefore, we do not know why the AI agents chose this strategy or whether it was successful.

The RubyGems team stopped new user sign-ups for four days to stem the tide of packages from the agents’ accounts. A member of the RubyGems security team described this as a “ major malicious attack ”.

Security companies termed the incident the “ GemStuffer campaign ”, while also noting confusion at the purpose of the attack. The malicious packages uploaded were used to retrieve information from UK local government sites – data that was available to the public. One news outlet writes: “It's not clear what exactly the end goals are, as the information appears to be publicly accessible anyway.”

We thank Jonas Wiedermann-Möller ( @j0wimo ) for discovering that agents had likely uploaded packages to RubyGems. We are also grateful to Alicja Piecha ( @she_llac ) for conducting an independent preliminary analysis of the agents’ use of RubyGems We were not aware of Alicja’s work prior to publishing our report. and for coordinating the Swarmchasers community.

We believe that this incident was the result of an OpenAI agent swarm. Our main sources of evidence are:

The June agents were accessing 49 of the same files as the wiki agents, which OpenAI has confirmed were theirs.

The May agents were accessing different files (mostly local UK government data), but these files are very similar in character to those pursued by the wiki agents. Moreover, they use the same retrieval methods. 1,397 packages mention r.jina.ai , which was used heavily by the agents on the wiki. We also see that many packages mention example.com , which wiki agents used to test their posting ability.

Our understanding from talking to people in the RubyGems community is that OpenAI never informed them that they were responsible for this attack.

Note: After publishing this report, we were informed that X user @she_llac independently discovered that the agents were using RubyGems’ build system in order to fetch packages and shared this on Discord prior to us publishing. We’re grateful for @she_llac’s work in both discovering this and in coordinating a community of people to look for more rogue agents.

Whenever you publish a package (also known as a gem) to RubyGems, and submit a request, the site RubyDoc.info builds and hosts documentation for it.

The process of building documentation for a gem involves evaluating a user-specified `.yardopts` file, which allows linking to Ruby scripts intended to help with this process. In the GemStuffer campaign, the agents abused this to gain arbitrary remote code execution on the RubyDoc.info ’s servers.

We know that this was the intended pathway of the agents because they (rather transparently) told us so.

In the now-rescinded gem zzsouthrunner (which notably shares the ZZ naming scheme that both the wiki agents and Huggingface ones used), the agents leave the following comment on top of the linked payload:

We know that over a hundred packages used the following exploitation path:

Additionally, once the AIs got arbitrary RCE on the build environment, they would sometimes use the build environment to attempt to steal other users’ API keys (though we are unsure if they succeeded or not). This is discussed more in the following section.

The agents clearly regarded what they were doing as hacking. Agents used file names like hack.rb , evil.rb , inject.rb , exploit.rb , and ssrf.rb . ( SSRF stands for “Server-Side Request Forgery”, a type of security vulnerability). They also dubbed packages conspicuous titles like pwnp999, exfiltestwand3, hacksvn1778554764, and lambproxyhackabcxyz. Comments such as “# malicious probe” or “#hack” are littered across the campaign.

At some points, the agents attempted to be covert. We found multiple packages that would disarm themselves to hide their payload in the next version. They uploaded one package with the comment “ # disable evil in next version and bump version”, which after execution would modify the package to remove the malicious code initially inserted. Another such package (lambethcalcqzewgt) follows the same self-disarming pattern. (Fortunately, they still uploaded these files and comments publicly, so they were not very successful at their “covert” behavior).

One particularly concerning finding is that agents attempted to exploit a vulnerability on May 12th that was only discovered in July .

RubyGems’ servers were set up to improperly cache users’ sign-in information. When a user with a legacy version ran `gem signin`, their key would be cached by the CDN Content Delivery Network; a group of servers spread across geographic areas that store website content for the sake of speeding up loading times , and served to others. This meant that when someone sent a GET request to `/api/v1/api_key` on the same physical CDN node for up to an hour after the user signed in, it would leak their API key. By querying this endpoint while unauthenticated, an attacker could steal a random user’s key.

According to RubyGems’ security advisory , 18% of user sign-ins (as of July) still used affected versions of the package manager `gem`. We think that there were a little less than 10 affected sign-ins per day on average, which this attack’s chance at succeeding would depend heavily on.

We found that at least six packages [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] used this vulnerability. One example is the package “ slnleaker5 .”

We stress that the agents were attempting to exploit a novel security vulnerability in order to steal people’s RubyGems API keys . We do not know if this attempt succeeded, but we have confirmed with the RubyGems team that this was a viable pathway to obtain API keys illicitly if a user with the right version of RubyGems was logging in within an hour of the attack on the right internal CDN node. However, the RubyGems team said they had conducted extensive reviews and found no evidence that this pathway was exploited in the past. However, we can’t rule it out entirely.

Another bug in rubygems.org allowed agents to get working API keys by registering accounts, but not verifying their email addresses, which was unintended behavior. The fix for this was submitted on May 11th, and merged to production on May 12th, 2026.

Our understanding is that agents used large numbers of disposable email addresses to create accounts, in addition to using this bypass, so that they could publish gems. On May 16th, registration with disposable emails was disabled as well.

The AI agents created a set of packages which used RubyGems’ webhook system as a way to store data. Instead of storing data normally, they encoded it in URLs so that future models could see them. We’re not sure why they did it this way (as opposed to storing data normally, or e.g. in a comment in the file).

We’ll now give our (relatively more technical) summary of how this worked in the following case: southpxdatapp6pi .

Normally, a RubyGems webhook is just a stored URL: a user registers a URL and RubyGems can contact that URL when a gem is published. In this case, the agents used the URL itself as a data store. The method was as follows.

First, the code fetches a webpage containing data useful to its task (in this case, UK local government data). It keeps the HTTP status code (giving information about whether the request succeeded) and the response body, containing the relevant information.

Next, the code compresses and then encodes this data using URL-safe-Base64 (which is an encoding scheme that only uses characters allowed to be placed in a URL). Despite the compression, the encoded data may still be too long to store in a single URL, so the code splits it into chunks of 220 characters or less.

It then registers a RubyGems webhook for each chunk, placing that chunk as part of the URL. Conceptually, the outputs look like these:

The indexes in the URL let future AIs reconstruct the correct chunk ordering. Then, any future model with access to this RubyGems account could list these webhooks and then access the data. (The agents literally used example.com in the encoding).

This incident primarily occurred in May. In response to this, RubyGems temporarily disabled new user signups from May 12 to May 16. Afterwards, RubyGems introduced additional security measures, such as requiring non-disposable, verified emails, as well as adding rate limits to new signups. This appears to have prevented most agent activity for the rest of May (aside from a small amount of activity on the 26th).

Over 3 hours on June 18th, agent activity on RubyGems briefly increased again with agents publishing 83 gems over 3 hours.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news. Zelensky propone di incontrare Putin al G20 di Miami a dicembre. Ma il Cremlino frena
items.summary: Prudenza da Mosca su possibile incontro tra i due presidenti: “Presenza di Putin al summit nemmeno discussa”. In Bulgaria esplode deposito di armi destinate a kIEV
items.content:
Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky si è detto aperto a incontrare Vladimir Putin in occasione del G20 di Miami a dicembre : “Dobbiamo andarci. Dobbiamo incontrarci, parlare e prendere decisioni", ha affermato Zelensky spiegando che ciò che direbbe a Putin conta meno dei risultati. "Non è una questione di parole. Ciò che gli dirò o ciò che lui vorrà dire a me non conta. Contano i risultati. Tutto qui". Il Cremlino si è finora rifiutato di dire se Putin parteciperà al summit.

Nuova notte di attacchi incrociati tra Russia e Ucraina. Un missile russo ha colpito un impianto industriale a Kryvyj Rih , provocando un morto e due feriti. Droni ucraini hanno invece preso di mira Tolyatti e Taganrog , in territorio russo: colpito un impianto chimico strategico e segnalati incendi nei pressi di un aeroporto e di uno stabilimento automobilistico. Esplosioni anche a Odessa dopo un raid aereo russo.

Il Cremlino: “La presenza di Putin a G20 nemmeno ancora discussa”

Zelensky propone di incontrare Putin al G20 di Miami a dicembre

Putin: “Il dispiegamento di forze europee in Ucraina è ingresso in guerra”

Attacco russo con droni su Zaporizhzhia, un morto e un ferito

"Le forze di guerra elettronica deviano ogni giorno centinaia di droni russi". Lo ha scritto il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky su X in occasione della Giornata delle forze di guerra elettronica, sottolineando il ruolo svolto da queste unità nella difesa del Paese. Secondo Zelensky, la guerra elettronica protegge anche le comunicazioni e consente alle unità ucraine di rimanere meno visibili al nemico. In un momento in cui l'Ucraina deve fare i conti con una carenza di intercettori, il lavoro di queste forze permette di proteggere "migliaia e migliaia di vite ucraine" che altrimenti sarebbero raggiunte dai droni Shahed russi e iraniani a propulsione a reazione. Zelensky ha ringraziato i militari per il lavoro svolto quotidianamente, sottolineando il loro contributo all'innovazione e alla capacità di complicare i piani delle forze russe.

Today is Electronic Warfare Forces Day. A day honoring the people whose work often goes unnoticed, but what matters is that its results are always there – at the front and in the rear. Every day, our warriors in the Electronic Warfare Forces divert hundreds of Russian drones… pic.twitter.com/Lx31FsxIoI

Cremlino a Zelensky: “Se vuole incontrare Putin venga a Mosca”

Se Volodymyr Zelensky desidera realmente incontrare Vladimir Putin, può recarsi a Mosca, come già proposto dal presidente russo. Lo ha dichiarato il portavoce del Cremlino Dmitri Peskov, commentando la disponibilità espressa dal leader ucraino a incontrare Putin a margine del vertice del G20 di Miami.

Ambasciatore ucraino in Italia: “L’unica via d'uscita è la trattativa a livello di leader”

"La natura ucraina non è quella di fare la guerra, vogliamo arrivare alla pace e per questo ci vogliono le trattative. Ma non possono spaventarci dicendoci 'le facciamo solo quando uscite dal Donbass', ma non è così, perché se si esce dal Donbass i russi continueranno a conquistare (territorio), ad avvicinarsi più verso l'Europa occidentale. Per questo la via d'uscita è quella della trattativa a livello di leader". Lo ha detto l'ambasciatore dell'Ucraina in Italia, Ihor Brusylo , intervenendo alla Conferenza europea di Ventotene per la libertà e la democrazia. Il diplomatico ha poi ricordato che "la garanzia principale è l'adesione all'Unione europea perché questa è anche la protezione di tutta l'Europa".

Un incendio seguito da diverse esplosioni ha distrutto nella notte un deposito di munizioni della società bulgara Emko, fornitrice di armi all'Ucraina. L'episodio arriva appena un mese dopo un incidente analogo in un'altra struttura vicina della stessa azienda. Tra le ipotesi al vaglio degli investigatori figura anche quella del sabotaggio. L'incendio è scoppiato intorno alle 23:20 locali , le 22:20, in un deposito di Gorni Varpishta, nella Bulgaria centrale, dove erano conservate munizioni e polvere da sparo. Lo ha riferito la televisione pubblica Bnt. Le fiamme e le detonazioni non hanno provocato feriti. I lavoratori presenti sono stati evacuati, mentre tre squadre di vigili del fuoco sono intervenute per spegnere un incendio boschivo innescato dalle esplosioni e successivamente posto sotto controllo.

Il Cremlino: “La presenza di Putin a G20 nemmeno ancora discussa”

"La possibilità che il presidente russo Vladimir Putin partecipi al prossimo vertice del G20 negli Stati Uniti non è ancora stata nemmeno discussa". Lo ha detto il consigliere di Putin per la politica estera, Yuri Ushakov , citato dalla Tass. "Sono stati invitati tutti, per quanto ne so, tranne il Sudafrica, purtroppo. Qui il lavoro prosegue a livello di esperti. I nostri continuano a lavorare ai documenti per il vertice, quindi tutto procede come di consueto", ha affermato. "Quanto alla possibilità di un viaggio di Putin, non abbiamo nemmeno affrontato la questione"

Peskov: “Aumentato impegno Usa per la pace, speriamo dia frutti”

"Gli sforzi americani per la pace in Ucraina si sono intensificati e la Russia spera che diano i loro frutti". Lo ha dichiarato il portavoce del Cremlino, Dmitry Peskov, al quotidiano russo Izvestia. "Gli americani continuano i loro sforzi per la pace, per i quali siamo molto grati, e che ora si sono ulteriormente intensificati. Speriamo sinceramente che questi sforzi diano i loro frutti", ha dichiarato Peskov.

Rispetto alle relazioni commerciali con Washington, "Mosca riscontra un grande interesse da parte del mondo imprenditoriale nel riprendere la cooperazione tra Russia e Stati Uniti", ha aggiunto Peskov.

Il numero dei feriti nell'attacco russo nella regione di Odessa è salito a 23. Come riporta Ukrinform, l'annuncio è stato dato dal capo del dipartimento di polizia dell'oblast di Odessa, Oleh Kiper, tramite Telegram. Sette adulti e un neonato di cinque mesi sono stati ricoverati in ospedale. La regione di Odessa è stata colpita da un massiccio attacco missilistico e con droni. Secondo Kiev, i russi hanno preso di mira infrastrutture civili.

Putin: “Non minacciamo l'Europa, il conflitto parte da Stati Ue”

La Russia non minaccia i Paesi europei e non avrebbe alcun motivo per entrare in conflitto con loro. Lo ha detto il presidente russo Vladimir Putin a New Delhi, come riporta Ntv, accusando invece gli Stati europei di provocare un possibile scontro con Mosca. "La Russia non minaccia nessun Paese europeo e non abbiamo alcun motivo per un conflitto con loro", ha affermato Putin, sostenendo che con la fine della Seconda guerra mondiale "tutte le questioni sono state risolte". "Vogliono rivedere i risultati della Seconda Guerra mondiale? A cosa stanno spingendo i popoli dei loro Paesi? A una guerra con la Federazione Russa?", ha aggiunto.

Zelensky propone di incontrare Putin al G20 di Miami a dicembre

Volodymyr Zelensky è pronto ad andare al G20 di Miami se anche il presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, parteciperà al vertice dei leader in programma a dicembre. E' quanto afferma il presidente ucraino in un'intervista alla Deutsche Welle. "Sì, certo. Dobbiamo andarci. Dobbiamo incontrarci, parlare e prendere decisioni", ha affermato Zelensky spiegando che ciò che direbbe a Putin conta meno dei risultati. "Non è una questione di parole. Ciò che gli dirò o ciò che lui vorrà dire a me non conta. Non conta. [...] Contano i risultati. Tutto qui". Il Cremlino si è finora rifiutato di dire se Putin volerà a Miami per il G20.

Putin: “Il dispiegamento di forze europee in Ucraina è ingresso in guerra”

"Il dispiegamento di forze europee in Ucraina significherebbe l'entrata dei rispettivi Paesi in guerra con la Russia". Lo ha dichiarato il presidente russo Vladimir Putin a margine del summit dei Brics a New Delhi.

Un piccolo gruppo di sviluppatori, probabilmente freelance e attivi in Russia , ha utilizzato il chatbot di intelligenza artificiale Claude per realizzare il software di uno sciame autonomo di droni kamikaze con visuale in prima persona . Lo ha riferito Anthropic, la società che ha sviluppato il sistema, secondo quanto riporta il Guardian . Secondo un rapporto di 154 pagine dell'azienda sugli utilizzi illeciti di Claude, il software comprendeva funzioni per la guida nella fase terminale, la selezione degli obiettivi e il coordinamento tra diversi velivoli. Lo sciame era progettato per individuare autonomamente i bersagli e schiantarsi contro di essi per esplodere, senza che un essere umano adottasse la decisione finale. Durante la programmazione, gli sviluppatori hanno indicato ripetutamente come obiettivo una località nella regione ucraina di Donetsk. Il gruppo avrebbe utilizzato reti Vpn per aggirare i blocchi geografici imposti da Anthropic.

Le forze russe hanno colpito in Ucraina un'azienda a Kryvyi Rih, uccidendo una persona e ferendone altre due. Lo ha riferito su Telegram Oleksandr Hanzha, capo dell'Amministrazione militare regionale di Dnipropetrovsk, secondo quanto riportato da Ukrinform. "Il nemico ha colpito un impianto industriale a Kryvyi Rih. Una persona è rimasta uccisa e altre due ferite", si legge nel post.

items.summary: Pezeshkian: “Il Medio Oriente non ha bisogno di un poliziotto Usa”. Attacco all’oleodotto saudita, Riad: “I droni sono partiti dall’Iraq”
items.content:
L’Arabia Saudita ha chiuso temporaneamente l’ oleodotto Est-Ovest , una delle principali vie per aggirare il blocco dello Stretto di Hormuz. L’Iraq ha confermato che i droni sono partiti dal proprio territorio e ha rimosso il comandante responsabile della provincia di Missan. Riad, su richiesta di Baghdad, ha deciso per ora di non reagire. Intanto diverse navi russe con carichi militari sono state segnalate nel Mediterraneo, due delle quali dirette verso Tartus, in Siria. Secondo Anthropic, l’Iran avrebbe utilizzato la sua intelligenza artificiale Claude per pianificare attacchi contro navi militari statunitensi.

Trump: “Gli Houthi ci hanno chiamato, non vogliono uno scontro con noi”

Pezeshkian: "Non abbiamo bisogno di un gendarme per la regione”

Arabia Saudita, attacco all’oleodotto Est-Ovest. Riad: “I droni sono partiti dall’Iraq”

Anthropic accusa l'Iran: “Ha preso di mira navi della Marina Usa con l'IA”

Reuters: “La Casa Bianca valuta il Defense Production Act per aumentare raffinazione petrolifera”

Scontro armato nel Belucistan: almeno 7 morti di cui 3 pasdaran

Almeno sette persone, tra cui tre membri dei pasdaran, sono rimaste uccise sabato durante scontri armati nella città di Saravan - nell'ambito di un'operazione contro una "cellula terroristica" - segnando l'ultimo episodio di violenza nella turbolenta provincia del Sistan-Baluchistan, dove gli scontri si sono intensificati negli ultimi giorni. "Tre membri delle Guardie rivoluzionarie sono stati uccisi in un'operazione durata fino a mezzogiorno di oggi", ha annunciato il corpo militare d'èlite iraniano in una dichiarazione citata dalla televisione di Stato.

La Nato e i Paesi europei sono stati "molto deludenti sotto molti aspetti" durante la guerra con l'Iran. Lo ha dichiarato il presidente degli Stati Uniti, Donald Trump parlando a Dublino. "La Nato non ha voluto aiutarci con lo Stretto di Hormuz, anche se noi non riceviamo petrolio dallo Stretto", ha affermato. Trump ha inoltre sostenuto che in Iran "tutti hanno visto il predominio dell'equipaggiamento militare americano". "Abbiamo eliminato ogni mina. Non ci sono più mine là fuori", ha assicurato.

Iran: “Tre membri delle forze di sicurezza e 4 terroristi morti in scontri nel sud-est”

Le Guardie Rivoluzionarie iraniane hanno dichiarato oggi che "oggi è stata smantellata una squadra terroristica professionista che intendeva compiere un attentato a Saravan, nella provincia del Sistan-Baluchistan. Almeno quattro membri del gruppo sono rimasti uccisi negli scontri". Nell'episodio "sono morti anche tre membri delle Guardie Rivoluzionarie", hanno aggiunto, secondo quanto riportato dall'agenzia Tasnim

A Trump viene chiesto cosa direbbe a chi, in Irlanda, sostiene che gli Stati Uniti stiano favorendo il genocidio a Gaza e l'occupazione illegale di territori in Cisgiordania da parte di Israele. "Abbiamo spento l'incendio", risponde Trump, aggiungendo che gli USA hanno ottenuto il ritorno in Israele di tutti gli ostaggi presi durante l'attacco del 7 ottobre. Aggiunge che gli Stati Uniti hanno "favorito una sorta di pace". Martin interviene affermando di aver discusso con Trump della necessità di garantire continui aiuti umanitari a Gaza. "Lo faremo, senza dubbio", aggiunge Trump.

Trump: “Teheran probabilmente responsabile per l’attacco all’oleodotto saudita”

L'Iran è "probabilmente" responsabile dell'attacco con droni contro l'oleodotto saudita East-West. Lo ha detto il presidente americano Donald Trump rispondendo a una domanda dei giornalisti a Dublino, come riporta Sky News. "Beh, penso che probabilmente lo siano", ha risposto Trump alla domanda se Teheran fosse responsabile dell'attacco. L'oleodotto East-West è stato chiuso dopo essere stato colpito da droni partiti dal territorio iracheno, provocando interruzioni a una delle principali infrastrutture utilizzate dall'Arabia Saudita per le esportazioni di greggio

Trump: “Gli Houthi ci hanno chiamato, non vogliono uno scontro con noi”

Gli Houthi hanno preso contatto con gli Stati Uniti per assicurare che non cercano uno scontro con loro. A riferirlo è stato il presidente americano Donald Trump, dopo l'incontro a Dublino con il premier irlandese Michel Martin. "Gli Houthi ci hanno chiamato, non vogliono uno scontro con noi", ha spiegato, "e non vogliono che li mettiamo nel mirino. Stanno lasciando passare la maggior parte delle navi senza ostacoli".

Pezeshkian: "Non abbiamo bisogno di un gendarme per la regione”

"La solidarietà tra i Paesi musulmani è essenziale nelle circostanze attuali". Lo ha dichiarato il presidente iraniano Masoud Pezeshkian durante un incontro con il premier malese a margine del vertice dei Brics. "Non abbiamo bisogno di un gendarme per la regione. L'integrità territoriale e la sicurezza della regione possono essere garantite soltanto dai suoi principali attori e dai Paesi della regione", ha aggiunto Pezeshkian.

"Andrà tutto bene". Così il presidente americano Donald Trump ha risposto a una domanda dei giornalisti sulla situazione in Iran prima di un incontro con la presidente dell'Irlanda Catherine Connolly nella residenza di Aras an Uachtarain a Dublino.

Iran: “Per ora nessun negoziato con Usa finché nostre condizioni non saranno soddisfatte”

L'Iran non intende trattare con gli americani fino a quando non vi saranno le dovute premesse. Ad assicurarlo è stato Ebrahim Azizi, capo della commissione Sicurezza nazionale del parlamento iraniano. "Nessun negoziato. Finché le condizioni dell'Iran non saranno soddisfatte, i colloqui sono inutili", ha scritto su X.

Il ministro degli Esteri iraniano: “Incontro di lunedì in Oman è una pietra miliare per la sicurezza del Golfo”

L'incontro di lunedì in Oman tra i paesi rivieraschi "è una pietra miliare per garantire la stabilità e la sicurezza della regione del Golfo Persico". Ad assicurarlo è stato il portavoce del ministero degli Esteri iraniano, Esmaeil Baqaei.

"Non cerchiamo la guerra nè vogliamo che continui. Nonostante tutte le ingiustizie subite dal nostro popolo, diamo priorità alla pace". Lo ha dichiarato il presidente iraniano, Masoud Pezeshkian, a margine del summit dei Brics a New Delhi. "Non abbiamo bisogno di un gendarme nella regione. L'integrità territoriale degli Stati e la sicurezza regionale possono essere garantite soltanto dagli attori della regione stessa", ha aggiunto. "Non abbiamo alcun problema con i nostri fratelli musulmani e con i Paesi vicini. E' Washington che cerca di trasformarci in nemici", ha evidenziato ancora Pezeshkian.

Il presidente libanese Joseph Aoun ha visitato a sorpresa Nabatiyeh, nel sud del Paese, città situata a pochi chilometri da una posizione strategica di Hezbollah recentemente conquistata e fatta esplodere dall'esercito israeliano. Secondo i media ufficiali libanesi, Aoun è arrivato senza preavviso, accompagnato da responsabili della sicurezza, e ha espresso solidarietà agli abitanti che lo hanno accolto. Il presidente ha visitato anche l'ospedale governativo di Nabatiyeh, elogiando il personale che continua a "rischiare la vita" per garantire l'assistenza sanitaria in una zona dalla quale è fuggita gran parte della popolazione.

"Oggi l'Iran resta saldo di fronte agli Stati Uniti e al regime sionista e non cederà alle loro prepotenze". Lo afferma il presidente, Masoud Pezeshkian, incontrando esponenti religiosi e del mondo degli affari indiani nella tarda serata di ieri, a margine del Forum Brics a Nuova Delhi. "Questi sedicenti paladini dei diritti umani sono, in realtà, attori malevoli che ci etichettano come terroristi", ha aggiunto, citato dall'agenzia Irna, sottolineando: "Stiamo pagando il prezzo di questa posizione, eppure, finché vivremo, perseguiremo la verità e la giustizia e non ci piegheremo all'oppressione, alla tirannia o alle prepotenze".

L'Iraq chiude la frontiera con l'Iran dopo attacco a oleodotto saudita

L'Iraq ha ordinato la chiusura del valico di frontiera di Shalamcheh, tra Iraq e Iran, come misura precauzionale in seguito ai recenti attacchi con droni contro l'Arabia Saudita: lo hanno riferito a Reuters due fonti della sicurezza. Secondo le fonti, è in corso un'operazione su larga scala per dare la caccia agli autori dell'attacco contro l'Arabia Saudita.

Ft: gli Usa limitano il transito da Hormuz perché “la notte non è sicura”

Gli Stati Uniti hanno chiesto alle navi che intendono attraversare lo Stretto di Hormuz di navigare in due fasce orarie variabili, e non solo di notte, al fine di garantire il passaggio. Lo riporta il Financial Times, spiegando che la misura decisa da Washington segue gli attacchi iraniani contro le navi a Hormuz. Da alcune comunicazioni inviate ai consulenti del traffico marittimo, scrive il Financial Times, sembra che la modifica delle fasce orarie sia avvenuta intorno all'inizio di settembre. Un'e-mail affermava che le navi non sono obbligate a navigare nell'orario specificato, ma "è raccomandato per un supporto ottimale". Un'altra e-mail osservava che "il passaggio durante le ore notturne non si è dimostrato il momento più sicuro della giornata".

items.title: Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane
items.summary: The Iran-backed Houthis are also reported to have seized Perim - a strategic island on the major shipping route.
items.content:
Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.

The Iran-backed group seized Perim Island at the mouth of the waterway in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a source from Yemen's internationally recognised government told the BBC.

It comes a day after the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, according to military sources. A Yemeni military official told the AFP news agency the Houthis now control the entire coastline.

The Houthis earlier said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis during their rapid advance, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News - the BBC's media partner in North America.

Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.

A senior Trump administration official later told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."

On Friday, Yemeni pro-government forces withdrew from Perim (also known as Mayyun).

Witnesses and news agencies reported that Houthi forces moved on to the island.

The Houthis later issued a statement, saying that their military operation to expel Saudi-backed forces had been a "success" and that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the "large-scale" military operation was launched on 3 September due to Saudi Arabia's "blatant aggression" against "our dear people".

Sarea also said the Houthis had expelled "Saudi enemy" forces from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, claiming that hundreds of troops had been killed, wounded or captured.

The Houthi statement, however, did not mention Perim Island.

Saudi Arabia has not publicly commented on the latest developments.

Perim Island sits at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has become increasingly important following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - another crucial waterway - in the conflict between the US and Iran.

Saudi Arabia has been relying on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait for shipping oil to customers in Asia.

The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.

Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced in Yemen since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.

A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi foreign affairs ministry said on Friday that drones from Iraq had targeted the country's East-West oil pipeline, forcing it to be closed as a "precautionary measure" and injuring several people.

Iraq's government condemned the attack and its prime minister has launched an investigation.

In a statement, the prime minister's office said the operations commander in the Maysan governorate - a province which borders Iran - had been removed from his post following confirmation the drone attack had originated from that region.

Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said that, following a call from Iraq's prime minister, it had chosen not to respond to the attacks at this stage.

Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war

Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities

Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes

At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated with Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

On Friday, the IOM said the number was "alarmingly rising by the hour".

Amy Pope, IOM director general, said: "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left."

The Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government in 2015, triggering Saudi military intervention in the civil war.

The group currently control much of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. A truce that had largely held for more than four years effectively collapsed in July.

Project Blinkenlights turns buildings into giant interactive displays. What started in 2001 as the Chaos Computer Club 's birthday present to itself became a series of light installations on three continents — the whole story is told in the project overview .

items.title: Con Michael Kors al MoMa tra modernismi e Matisse
items.summary: Il preppy di Hilfiger torna a casa al Plaza, Ralph "romantico irriverente"
items.content: Tre grandi firme della moda di New York continuano a dare la linea in fatto di stile: Michael Kors, Tommy Hilfiger e Ralph Lauren hanno dato il via alla prima fashion week della stagione presentando capi che resistono al passare del tempo. "Edie Sedgwick e Nico, le icone della factory di Andy Warhol, potrebbero essere con noi oggi col loro look è assolutamente senza tempo", spiega il 67enne Kors presentando la sfilata che oggi, come l'anno scorso al Lincoln Center, lo ha portato nei giardini del MoMA. Le idee di riferimento sono il modernismo e architetture come il Breuer Building su Madison Avenue o il terminal TWA di Eero Saarinen, edifici che hanno resistito alla prova degli anni: "Per me, qualunque cosa faccia, deve superare la prova del tempo, ma anche dare gioia, sollevare lo spirito, cambiare il tuo sguardo: come il mix di persone che incontri in un museo o a un vernissage, e ci trovi Bushwick insieme a Park Avenue". Ed ecco dunque capi dalla sartoria asciutta, netta, stretta, accompagnati da accenti architettonici nei gioielli, negli orecchini a paletta, nelle righe, nei lampi di colore. Tante minigonne e scarpe comode che soppiantano le sneaker: "C'è ottimismo, ma è l'ottimismo realistico di una città. Oggi ne abbiamo tutti bisogno". Ispirato dallo sfondo, Kors trasforma la pittura in ricamo: in un cappotto un motivo floreale di organza di seta e chiffon sfilacciati a mano sembra una pennellata, mentre le sedie disegnate da Breuer o da Mies van der Rohe declinano i tacchi delle scarpe e gli inserti metallici delle borse. C'è una pochette troppo minuscola per metterci il telefono: "Alla proprietaria basta una Amex Black. Il cellulare ce l'ha in mano e, se serve, lo dà a qualcun altro". Un abito da sera nero disegna sul corpo curve alla Matisse giocando con linee curve e paillette stropicciate a mano e poi leggermente fuse con il calore. Dal Moma al Plaza sono pochi isolati: per il 75enne Hilfiger è un ritorno a casa. Il leggendario albergo - dove lo stesso Tommy ha vissuto con la famiglia - è lo scenario di una rilettura moderna dello stile preppy, facendo incontrare la tradizione uptown e il cool downtown sotto lo stesso tetto. "Da 40 anni mi ispira lo stile dei newyorchesi, il modo in cui le persone di questa città prendono i classici e li fanno propri", ha detto lo stilista che ha mixato le classiche icone Tommy rendendole più sofisticate per il presente. Kate Moss nel parterre, Gigi Hadid e Romeo Beckham ad aprire e chiudere la sfilata, il Plaza diventa così la porta girevole di una reinterpretazione del preppy americano in cui al caratteristico rosso, bianco e blu si affiancano gialli accesi e verdi vibranti. I capi della tradizione acquistano nuova vita attraverso motivi e stampe: dai rugby dress color-block alle camicie Oxford a righe Ithaca, fino ai tradizionali tartan utilizzati per blazer e giacche Ivy. Infine Ralph, che ha giocato d'anticipo alla Jack Shainman Gallery downtown con ospiti vip come Viola Davis, Eiza Gonzalez, Cynthia Erivo, Rachel Brosnahan e Elizabeth Debicki. Ralph, 86 anni, ha definito "un'interpretazione irriverente del romantico" la sfilata con abiti da sera in velluto lavorati con effetti di trasparenza, jeans sfilacciati e portati bassi sui fianchi e un richiamo ironico alle cravatte extra-large con cui lo stilista diede inizio al suo impero ben 59 anni fa.

items.title: Tragic death of woman who testified against father in notorious mafia murder of mother
items.summary: Denise Cosco testified against the powerful 'Ndrangheta clan and her own father over the murder of her mother in Italy.
items.content:
A woman who testified against her own father after her mother was murdered in a notorious mafia killing in Italy is believed to have taken her own life.

Denise Cosco was found critically injured on Sunday and died later in hospital in Rome.

Her mother Lea Garofalo, who was killed in 2009, became a powerful symbol of resistance to the mafia after turning witness for the state against the 'Ndrangheta clan in southern Italy.

Those close to Cosco recall her bravery in speaking out at her father's trial, but also her tremendous struggle in the years that followed.

At 35, she died at the same age her mother was when she was murdered.

Enza Rando, a senator and anti-mafia lawyer who represented Cosco at the murder trial, described her death as "a profound wound for the entire country", and proof that the mafia not only kills, but creates "true monsters in the lives and souls" of those who survive.

Francesca Rispoli, co-president of the anti-mafia organisation Libera, said the death highlighted the struggle experienced by many who break with organised crime.

"The mafia, it's not just something physical. You can leave. You can change your name," she told the BBC. "But there is still a tie, a family tie, that stays… deep inside and is impossible to overcome."

Cosco, like her mother, had lived under state protection with a new name and identity for many years.

But Rispoli said she remained extremely vulnerable and had reconnected with her father, Carlo Cosco, in prison in recent years because, despite everything, she had felt a "hole in her life".

Friends say she struggled with mental health problems and addiction.

"Maybe this is a sign that those trying to lead another life need more support. Not just for one year – maybe their whole life," Rispoli argued, as organised crime groups in Italy – especially the 'Ndrangheta - involve close-knit family networks.

In Cosco's case, both her mother's family and her father were tied to the mafia.

She had always refused to believe her father's story that her mother had abandoned her to start a new life in Australia.

In fact, he had tricked Garofalo to a meeting, then had her strangled, her body dismembered then incinerated.

Several years later, a statement by one of the killers finally allowed police to recover some fragments of bone and a necklace, which Cosco identified.

At a public funeral in 2013, she spoke of her mother's courage in "putting herself on the line… for justice for all".

Her father and three accomplices were already serving life in prison.

At the trial, Cosco described herself as a "proud witness for justice" and said she had taken the difficult choice to testify – speaking from behind a screen – because she wanted "inner freedom to start over" with her life.

Prosecutors have now opened an investigation to determine whether there was any incitement to suicide and her phone has been seized for analysis.

Friends and supporters were due to gather in Milan on Friday evening to remember her near the spot where her mother was abducted.

"Denise's entire life revolved between the two extremes of courage and suffering," Luigi Ciotti, president of Libera wrote, calling that a difficult balance.

"Today, something in that fragile equilibrium was broken forever."

If you or someone you know are affected by the issues raised in this story, the BBC Action Line has information on organisations that can offer advice and support.

items.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
items.summary: The capture by the rebels of a stretch of Yemen's strategic coastline is the group's most impressive military coup for several years.
items.content:
The Houthis' lightning advance across the southern reaches of the Tihamah – Yemen's arid coastal plain – appears to have taken most observers by surprise.

Until recently, the anti-Houthi coalition known as the National Resistance held significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast. In a matter of days, much of this has fallen to the Houthis.

According to some estimates, the Iranian-backed rebels have captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's strategically important coastline.

It's the group's most impressive military coup for several years, proving that despite a civil war that has lasted 12 years, devastating Saudi air raids and attacks by American, Israeli and British forces, the Houthis remain a force to be reckoned with.

With their opponents stunned and demoralised, it's unlikely the Houthis will be dislodged any time soon.

Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane

Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes

"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.

As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.

"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."

Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".

In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.

Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.

President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.

According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.

Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".

But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.

Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.

Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".

With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.

For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

items.title: I spent $220 on Google app ads and 60% of the installs were robots
items.summary: Article URL: https://dayzlegame.com/blog/google-ads-bot-farm/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49662990 Points: 599 # Comments: 329
items.content:
I run a small puzzle app called Dayzle. I’m a numbers guy, so a marketing optimization problem is right up my alley. Two weeks ago I turned on a Google Ads campaign for Android at CA$40 a day, with the goal set to installs.

For the first few days it barely spent anything. I had a target cost per install of $1.50, and Google couldn’t find installs at that price. So, as a test, I removed the target. It immediately spent double my daily budget, CA$80, and reported 21 installs. I was excited. Then I checked my admin panel, which said 1. Turns out I didn’t need to be a numbers guy to see something didn’t add up.

The panel had missed them because old versions of the app don’t report an install date. When I went into the raw analytics there were 21 new Android devices that day, and 20 of them were running an old version of the app that the Play Store had stopped serving days earlier. You can’t get an old version from Play, so these phones got the app from somewhere else, even though every one of them said Google Play was the installer. Each opened the app once, spent zero seconds on any screen, and never came back. Twenty-eight phone models across nineteen states, which is a lot of variety for twenty phones that all did exactly the same thing.

Over the whole two weeks: 56 installs billed, 33 with that pattern, 7 more from countries the campaign wasn’t targeting, and 13 people. The 13 people finished 92 games between them, which is a nice signal that real people enjoyed what we’ve built.

The 33 weren’t behaving like people, so I suspected a bot farm, and the analytics export bears it out. Google optimizes for whatever goal you give it, and my goal was installs. This farm would watch the shortest video in my ad group, not click it, and then install our app from a saved copy of the file instead of from the store, because that’s faster and Play might notice. Google counts a view followed by an install as a conversion, so the irony is that the more the farm “installed” our app, the better it looked to Google’s algorithm, which sent more of my ads to the farm, which installed it more. A loop that guaranteed my ad spend was wasted.

Where I am now: waiting on Google’s answer to the invalid-traffic form, and the campaign’s goal is now “won a puzzle” instead of “opened the app”. It’s low effort to make a script open an app and click around; it’s higher effort to make one solve a Sudoku. The idea is just to make us more expensive to farm than the next app. That’s probably decent protection for an app my size. Larger apps are worth the extra effort, and I’d guess they see a lot more of this than they know. I’ll report back on the refund.

So I guess this is my PSA: if you’re relying on Google’s install count for your ads, it’s a real number, but it’s definitely worth digging into. If a bot farm can find my tiny ad budget, it can definitely find yours.

items.title: Litelm: LiteLLM Without the Bloat
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/kennethwolters/litelm Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49662767 Points: 153 # Comments: 51
items.content:
litellm's routing + translation in ~2,900 lines and 2 dependencies ( openai , httpx ).

litellm routes LLM calls across providers and translates between message formats. That core is buried under 100k+ LOC of proxy servers, caching layers, cost tracking, and dozens of features most users never touch. litelm extracts just the call path — model routing, message translation, streaming, tool use, embeddings — and nothing else. No Router class, no proxy, no caching.

Every function has an async variant: acompletion , aembedding , aresponses , atext_completion .

The API mirrors litellm — same function names, same arguments, same response types. If you're using litellm today, switching is s/litellm/litelm/ in your imports.

Routes to 19 providers via "provider/model-name" syntax. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works via api_base .

All provider errors are mapped to litelm's exception hierarchy:

litelm is human-directed, AI-assisted software. Much of the code was written with Claude Code using Claude Opus 4.6/4.7. Code written from 2026-05-14 onward is written through Pi using GPT-5.5. Compatibility claims are based on tests and maintainer review, not AI authorship.

Maintainer attestation, 2026-09-11: LiteLLM's routing/formatting changes were reviewed from 649eb2d through 9a715df2 . The audit triaged 360 core-path commits, inspected upstream tests for potentially relevant behavior, and fixed the resulting compatibility gaps test-first. Local scoped tests: 262 passed, 55 skipped ; all 45 available-provider live tests and all 10 DSPy smoke tests also passed with the current dependency lock.

This attests litelm's declared routing/formatting/DSPy surface only, not full litellm compatibility.

Alpha. 262 own tests passing. The current scoped LiteLLM 9a715df2 baseline has 75 passing ported tests and no remaining actionable assertion/runtime failures.

DSPy drop-in verified — all 7 execution paths proven live (Predict, CoT, typed signatures, streaming, embeddings, tool use, multi-output).

Live tests require API keys in .env.test . Skipped by default; run with -m live .
